hints: Focus on solubility trends down Group 2, they go opposite ways for sulfates and hydroxides.
Recall that $\text{BaSO}_4$ is famously insoluble while $\text{MgSO}_4$ is very soluble, so test 1 favours one ion.
Now flip it for hydroxides, $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble while $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble, so test 2 favours the other ion.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two solubility trends**

Think of Group 2 like a seesaw. Going down the group, sulfates get less soluble, but hydroxides get more soluble.

Trend summary:
$$\text{sulfate solubility: Mg}^{2+} > \text{Ca}^{2+} > \text{Sr}^{2+} > \text{Ba}^{2+}$$
$$\text{hydroxide solubility: Mg}^{2+} < \text{Ca}^{2+} < \text{Sr}^{2+} < \text{Ba}^{2+}$$

**Apply to test 1 with sulfate**

We add $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions. Barium forms a thick white precipitate, magnesium stays mostly in solution.

Reaction for barium:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Apply to test 2 with hydroxide**

We add $\text{OH}^-$ ions. This time it is the reverse. Magnesium forms a white precipitate, barium stays mostly in solution.

Reaction for magnesium:
$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$$

**Combine to choose**

Test 1 gives more precipitate with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Test 2 gives more precipitate with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. That matches one row in the table.

options.A: Test 1 is correct for $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, but test 2 is wrong. $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble, so $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ gives little or no precipitate with NaOH, while $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ gives a clear white precipitate.
options.B: Correct and reassuring. $\text{BaSO}_4$ is insoluble so test 1 favours $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, and $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble so test 2 favours $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. This perfectly shows the opposite solubility trends.
options.C: Both parts are reversed. This comes from mixing up the trends. Remember sulfates decrease in solubility down the group, hydroxides increase, so $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble.
options.D: Test 2 is correct for $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, but test 1 is wrong. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble in water, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ gives little precipitate with sulfate, while $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ gives abundant $\text{BaSO}_4$.
